Game Theory

This is an introductory text on game theory. Game theory asks one question: what happens when your best choice depends on what others do, and their best choice depends on what you do? Whether a prisoner confesses, how much two firms produce, what a bidder offers, how much a used-car seller asks: behind all of these is the same kind of problem.

The text starts with the simplest case, where everyone moves at once and knows the whole game. It then adds, one at a time, sequential moves, repeated interaction and private information, and each step brings a new equilibrium concept. Every concept comes with a small example you can work out with pen and paper.

You only need school algebra, a little differentiation (maximising a quadratic) and basic probability (expected values, conditional probability). Any other mathematics is explained where it is used.

What you will be able to do

After reading, you should be able to:

  1. Find dominant strategies and Nash equilibria in a payoff matrix, and explain why in the prisoners' dilemma everyone is rational and yet everyone loses (Ch. 2–3).
  2. Compute mixed-strategy equilibria: know when randomising is optimal and with which probabilities (Ch. 4).
  3. Analyse competition between a few firms: use best-response functions to find outputs, prices and profits in the Cournot, Bertrand and Stackelberg models, and explain why they differ (Ch. 5–7).
  4. Solve sequential games by backward induction, spot non-credible threats, and explain why repeated interaction can sustain cooperation (Ch. 9–10).
  5. Handle private information: update beliefs with Bayes' rule, compute optimal bids in auctions, and decide whether a signal (such as education) can separate different types of people (Ch. 8, 11, 12).

How to read.

  • Every chapter opens with an "Intuition" box that says in plain words which question the chapter answers. Read those first; the storyline is in them.
  • Every core concept is followed by a worked example with round numbers. Work it out yourself; every step is written out.
  • Paragraphs starting with "Proof" can be skipped on a first reading. Every important proof is preceded by an "In one sentence" summary, so you know why the result holds without the details.
  • Sections marked "Advanced" go beyond what later chapters need and can be skipped safely.
  • The last four chapters are a recap, common misconceptions, exercises with answers and a glossary.

Contents

  1. The big picture: what game theory studies
  2. Decision problems and expected utility
  3. Static games: representation and dominant strategies
  4. Nash equilibrium
  5. Mixed strategies
  6. Continuous strategies: quantity and price competition
  7. Pricing: escaping the Bertrand paradox
  8. Timing games: preemption and attrition
  9. Information structure: extensive form and Bayesian games
  10. Dynamic games: subgame perfection and backward induction
  11. Repeated games: how cooperation is sustained
  12. Auctions and mechanism design
  13. Dynamic games of incomplete information: perfect Bayesian equilibrium and signalling
  14. Recap: one storyline
  15. Common misconceptions
  16. Exercises with answers
  17. Glossary

Notation and overview

  • Players are numbered i=1,\dots,n; s_i is a strategy of player i and S_i is the set of all his strategies.
  • s=(s_1,\dots,s_n) is a strategy profile; s_{-i} means "the strategies of everyone except i", so s=(s_i,s_{-i}).
  • u_i(s) is player i's payoff (utility) under the profile s.
  • BR_i(s_{-i}) is i's best response to the others' strategies s_{-i}.
  • In a payoff matrix each cell reads "row player's payoff, column player's payoff".
  • p,q usually denote probabilities of an action in a mixed strategy; \delta\in(0,1) is the discount factor (one unit tomorrow is worth \delta today).
  • \mu denotes a belief (probabilities attached to things one cannot see); t_i denotes a type (information only the player knows, such as a valuation or ability).
  • Proofs end with \square.

0. The big picture: what game theory studies

Intuition. In an ordinary decision problem you face "nature": the weather, the market, luck. In a game you face people, and they are second-guessing you too. This chapter gives one picture of the whole text: two questions (who moves first? who knows what?) sort games into four kinds, and each kind has its own "equilibrium".

0.1 An everyday example

Driving to work, you wonder whether to take the main road or the side road. If everyone takes the main road it is jammed and the side road is clear; if everyone takes the side road it is the other way round. Your best choice depends on what others choose, and they are doing the same calculation. That is a game.

Unlike chess, games in economics are usually not zero-sum: both sides may want to avoid the jam, or to coordinate on the same technical standard. The job of game theory is to predict where rational people end up after second-guessing each other.

0.2 Game theory in three sentences

  1. A game consists of players, strategies and payoffs; if there is an order of moves or private information, we must also say who knows what, and when.
  2. An equilibrium is a situation in which, given what others do, nobody wants to change what he does on his own.
  3. Sequential moves require every threat and promise to be credible; private information requires everyone to hold reasonable beliefs about what they cannot see, updated in the light of observed actions.

0.3 Map of the text

Stage Question Everyday example Ch.
Decisions and static games Who chooses what when moves are simultaneous? prisoners' dilemma, where to meet 1–4
Oligopoly How do a few firms set output, price and timing? two airlines, two drug makers 5–7
Information structure How to draw "who knows what"? can you see the other's card? 8
Dynamic and repeated games Which threats are credible? Can long relationships sustain cooperation? price wars, cartels 9–10
Private information What if others know things I do not? auctions, used cars, education 11–12

0.4 Recurring characters

Alice and Bob appear throughout. Sometimes they are prisoners, sometimes firms, sometimes bidders. The names are just labels; what matters is that each pursues his own payoff and knows the other does too.

1. Decision problems and expected utility

Intuition. Before studying "person against person", get "person against nature" right: how does one person choose when the future is uncertain? The answer is to compare the expected utility of each choice. The tools of this chapter (utility functions, expectations, risk attitudes) run through the whole text, because in a game the other player's action is often just another uncertainty to you.

1.1 Three ingredients of a decision problem

A decision problem has three parts:

  • Actions: what can be chosen. The action set is A.
  • Outcomes: what each action leads to. The outcome set is X.
  • Preferences: a ranking of outcomes, written \succsim ("at least as good as").

Preferences are "rational" when they are complete (any two outcomes can be compared) and transitive (if a is at least as good as b and b at least as good as c, then a is at least as good as c).

If a function v satisfies "x\succsim y if and only if v(x)\ge v(y)", we say v is a payoff function representing the preference. With it, "choose your favourite" becomes "choose the largest number".

1.2 Uncertainty: actions become lotteries

Example (an MBA or not). An employee considers quitting to do an MBA. Over the next decade the demand for MBAs may be strong (probability \pi) or weak (probability 1-\pi).

  • MBA: present value of income 100 if demand is strong, 25 if weak.
  • No MBA: a sure 49.

Under uncertainty an action no longer leads to one outcome but to a lottery (a probability distribution over outcomes). The MBA lottery is "100 with probability \pi, 25 with probability 1-\pi"; the no-MBA lottery is "49 for sure".

1.3 Expected utility

Von Neumann–Morgenstern expected utility: give each outcome x a utility score u(x); the value of a lottery P is the expected score

U(P)=\sum_{x}p(x)\,u(x)=E_P[u(X)].

People choose the lottery with the highest expected utility. u is called the Bernoulli utility function, and its shape describes the attitude to risk:

Shape of u Risk attitude Meaning
straight line u(x)=x risk-neutral only the expected amount matters
concave (bending down), e.g. \sqrt x risk-averse prefers the expected value for sure to the gamble
convex (bending up) risk-loving prefers the gamble

Example continued (risk-neutral). u(x)=x: the MBA gives 100\pi+25(1-\pi)=25+75\pi; no MBA gives 49. The MBA is better if and only if

25+75\pi\ge 49\iff \pi\ge \frac{24}{75}=0.32.

Example continued (risk-averse). u(x)=\sqrt x: the MBA gives 10\pi+5(1-\pi)=5+5\pi; no MBA gives \sqrt{49}=7. The MBA is better if and only if 5+5\pi\ge 7, i.e. \pi\ge0.4.

The risk-averse employee is more cautious: she needs a higher chance of strong demand (0.4 rather than 0.32) before taking the risk.

2. Static games: representation and dominant strategies

Intuition. Now the opponent is a person. The simplest case is when everyone moves at the same time and everyone knows the rules and all payoffs. This chapter first shows how to write a game down as a table, then looks for the easiest kind of solution: a choice that is best whatever the others do (a dominant strategy). The prisoners' dilemma shows that when everyone picks what is best for himself, the result can be bad for all.

2.1 Normal form (the payoff matrix)

An n-player normal-form game (also called a strategic-form game) is written

G=\{(S_1,u_1),\dots,(S_n,u_n)\},

that is, each player's strategy set and payoff function. With two players and few strategies it can be drawn as a matrix: rows are player 1's strategies, columns are player 2's, and each cell holds both payoffs.

A strategy is a complete plan of action: it says what to do in every situation that can arise. In simultaneous-move games a strategy is simply an action; the difference shows up in Chapter 8 with sequential moves.

2.2 Best responses

If I knew what the other would do, what should I do?

Definition (best response). Given the others' strategies s_{-i}, s_i^* is a best response of i if it maximises i's payoff:

u_i(s_i^*,s_{-i})\ge u_i(s_i,s_{-i})\quad\text{for all } s_i\in S_i,

written s_i^*\in BR_i(s_{-i}).

The underlining method. In a matrix, for each column (each choice of the opponent) underline the row player's highest payoff; for each row underline the column player's highest payoff. We will use this trick again and again.

2.3 The prisoners' dilemma

Example. Alice and Bob are suspected of a serious crime and questioned separately. Each can fink (F, confess) or stay silent (S).

  • One finks, one stays silent: the finker goes free, the silent one gets 10 years.
  • Both fink: 9 years each.
  • Both silent: they can only be convicted of a minor offence, 1 year each.

Use minus the years in jail as payoffs:

Alice \ Bob F S
F −9, −9 0, −10
S −10, 0 −1, −1

Alice's best responses, step by step:

  • If Bob finks (column 1): Alice compares −9 and −10; finking is better, BR_A(F)=F.
  • If Bob is silent (column 2): Alice compares 0 and −1; finking is better, BR_A(S)=F.

Whatever Bob does, Alice should fink. Bob is in exactly the same position. So both fink and serve 9 years each. Yet if both stayed silent they would serve only 1 year each!

2.4 Dominant strategies and dominant-strategy equilibrium

Definition. s_i is a strictly dominant strategy if, against any strategies s_{-i} of the others, it is strictly better than every other strategy of i:

u_i(s_i,s_{-i})>u_i(s_i',s_{-i})\quad\text{for all } s_i'\ne s_i \text{ and all } s_{-i}.

If every player has a dominant strategy, the profile of these strategies is a dominant-strategy equilibrium.

The dominant-strategy equilibrium of the prisoners' dilemma is (F, F) with payoffs (-9,-9). Yet (S, S) makes both better off; we say (S, S) Pareto dominates (F, F).

The lesson of the prisoners' dilemma. Individual rationality (everyone plays his dominant strategy) does not guarantee collective rationality (an efficient outcome).

2.5 Two economic applications

Example (private provision of a public good). A street light is worth 3 each to Alice and Bob and costs 4. It is installed if someone volunteers to pay: if only one pays, he pays 4; if both pay, they pay 2 each. Strategies: volunteer (V) or free-ride (F).

Alice \ Bob F V
F 0, 0 3, −1
V −1, 3 1, 1

For instance in (V, F) Alice pays 4 and enjoys 3, getting −1, while Bob enjoys it for free, getting 3. Free-riding is dominant for each (0>−1, 3>1), so the light is never installed, although both would get 1 if both paid.

Example (doves and hawks in a duopoly). Each of two firms produces 1 unit (dove) or 2 units (hawk); producing a units costs a^2.

Case 1: total market revenue is fixed at 30, i.e. the price is p=30/(a+b).

  • Both produce 1: p=15, each earns 15-1=14.
  • One produces 2, the other 1: p=10; the 2-unit firm earns 20-4=16, the 1-unit firm 10-1=9.
  • Both produce 2: p=7.5, each earns 15-4=11.
Alice \ Bob hawk dove
hawk 11, 11 16, 9
dove 9, 16 14, 14

Hawk is dominant (11>9, 16>14); the equilibrium (hawk, hawk) gives (11, 11) and is Pareto dominated by (dove, dove) with (14, 14). Another prisoners' dilemma.

Case 2: total revenue is 12. The same computation gives

Alice \ Bob hawk dove
hawk 2, 2 4, 3
dove 3, 4 5, 5

Now dove is dominant, and the equilibrium (dove, dove) is also the best outcome. The "dilemma" has become a "delight". The same structure with different numbers can reverse the conclusion.

2.6 Iterated elimination of dominated strategies

Few games give every player a dominant strategy. A weaker approach: delete strategies that are obviously never used and see what is left.

Definition (weakly dominated). s_i is weakly dominated by s_i' if u_i(s_i',s_{-i})\ge u_i(s_i,s_{-i}) for all s_{-i}, with strict inequality for at least one s_{-i}.

Iterated elimination: delete a dominated strategy of some player, look for dominated strategies in the smaller table, delete again, and so on until each player has one strategy left.

Example (the order of elimination can change the result).

Row \ Column c_1 c_2 c_3
r_1 2, 12 1, 10 1, 12
r_2 0, 12 0, 10 0, 11
r_3 0, 12 1, 10 0, 13

Order 1: r_3 is weakly dominated by r_1 (2>0, 1=1, 1>0); delete it. In the remaining table c_3 is weakly dominated by c_1 (12=12, 12>11); delete it. Then delete r_2 (strictly dominated by r_1) and c_2 (10<12). The result is (r_1,c_1) with payoffs (2, 12).

Order 2: delete r_2 first (it is also dominated by r_1). With rows r_1,r_3 left, the column payoffs are: c_1 gives (12, 12), c_2 gives (10, 10), c_3 gives (12, 13). c_2 is dominated; delete it. c_1 is weakly dominated by c_3 (12=12, 12<13); delete it too. With only c_3 left, r_1 gives the row player 1 and r_3 gives 0; delete r_3. The result is (r_1,c_3) with payoffs (1, 12).

Conclusion: when deleting weakly dominated strategies, the result may depend on the order. (Deleting strictly dominated strategies does not have this problem: the end result is the same in any order.)

Solving a game this way rests on two informational assumptions: (i) everyone knows the whole payoff table; (ii) "nobody plays a dominated strategy" is common knowledge: everyone knows it, everyone knows that everyone knows it, and so on forever.

3. Nash equilibrium

Intuition. In most games nobody has a dominant strategy: my best choice really does depend on yours. Nash equilibrium gives a standard of "stability": everyone is best-responding to what the others do. Once there, nobody wants to change alone. The difficulty is that there may be several such points, and which one is reached depends on things outside the game (habit, communication, focal points).

3.1 Definition

Definition (Nash equilibrium). A strategy profile s^* is a Nash equilibrium if for every player i

u_i(s_i^*,s_{-i}^*)\ge u_i(s_i,s_{-i}^*)\quad\text{for all } s_i\in S_i.

In words, each player's strategy is a best response to the others' strategies; with the others fixed, nobody gains by changing alone.

In a matrix: a cell in which both payoffs are underlined is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.

3.2 The Battle of the Sexes: two equilibria

Example. Alice and Bob are to meet in the evening but got separated and cannot call each other. The choices are ballet (bal) or boxing (box). Above all they hate being apart; together, Alice prefers ballet and Bob prefers boxing.

Alice \ Bob bal box
bal 2, 1 0, 0
box 0, 0 1, 2

Best responses: BR_A(\text{bal})=\text{bal}, BR_A(\text{box})=\text{box}, and the same for Bob. Two cells are doubly underlined:

  1. (bal, bal) with payoffs (2, 1);
  2. (box, box) with payoffs (1, 2).

The game itself cannot tell which one will happen. If Alice had bought ballet tickets beforehand and told Bob, Bob would go to the ballet: this is a first-mover advantage (sequential moves are treated formally in Chapter 9).

3.3 The Stag Hunt and coordination

Example (Stag Hunt). Back to the duopoly, now with zero costs and demand p\cdot(a+b)^2=72.

  • Both produce 1: p=72/4=18, each earns 18.
  • Both produce 2: p=72/16=4.5, each earns 9.
  • One produces 2, the other 1: p=72/9=8; the 2-unit firm earns 16, the 1-unit firm 8.
Alice \ Bob hawk dove
hawk 9, 9 16, 8
dove 8, 16 18, 18

Two Nash equilibria: (hawk, hawk) with (9, 9) and (dove, dove) with (18, 18). Whatever the other chooses, it is best to choose the same. Such games are called coordination games: industry standards and investments that need several participants to succeed belong here.

Example (DVD or Blu-ray). Alice produces films, Bob produces players; they only make money with the same format (millions of dollars).

Alice \ Bob DVD Blu-ray
DVD 1, 1 −1, −1
Blu-ray −1, −1 3, 3

(Blu-ray, Blu-ray) Pareto dominates (DVD, DVD) and seems the obvious choice. But suppose Alice loses 500 instead of 1 when she chooses Blu-ray and Bob chooses DVD. Then if Alice thinks there is even a small chance that Bob makes a mistake, she will not dare to choose Blu-ray. The Pareto-better equilibrium need not be the less risky one.

3.4 Why study Nash equilibrium? Focal points

Nash equilibrium rests on two principles:

  1. Optimisation: everyone best-responds to his prediction of the others' behaviour;
  2. Correct predictions: these predictions match what the others actually do.

The first is almost the definition of economics; the second is a strong assumption. With several equilibria, people often coordinate on a focal point: a conventional, "natural" way to play.

Example (which side of the road).

A \ B left right
left 1, 1 0, 0
right 0, 0 1, 1

Both (left, left) and (right, right) are equilibria, and neither is better. Britain and Japan settled on left; France, Germany and the United States on right. In the driving game nobody cares which focal point is used; in the Battle of the Sexes the two prefer different ones, and then prior communication, a fairness rule ("we did what you wanted last time"), or public information (such as news that Blu-ray picture quality is better) can help coordinate.

4. Mixed strategies

Intuition. Some games have no doubly underlined cell at all. Matching pennies is the example: as soon as your choice can be predicted, your opponent exploits it. The fix is to randomise on purpose. In a mixed equilibrium each player's probabilities make the opponent exactly indifferent between his options, so the opponent has no reason to deviate either. The same idea applied to environmental inspection gives some very practical conclusions.

4.1 Matching pennies: no pure equilibrium

Example. Alice covers a coin (heads H or tails T) with her hand and Bob guesses. If Bob guesses right he wins a point; otherwise Alice wins a point.

Alice \ Bob H T
H 0, 1 1, 0
T 1, 0 0, 1

If Alice hides H, Bob guesses H; if Bob guesses H, Alice should hide T; if Alice hides T, Bob guesses T… and so on round and round. No cell is underlined twice: there is no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.

Just as x^2+1=0 has no real solution and mathematicians invented complex numbers, game theorists invented mixed strategies.

4.2 Definition of mixed strategies

Definition. A pure strategy assigns one action to each information set. A mixed strategy assigns a probability distribution over actions to each information set. A mixed strategy that gives positive probability to every action is completely mixed.

The point of matching pennies is to be unpredictable. The best way to be truly unpredictable is to hand the decision to a random device. The question is: with what probabilities?

4.3 Solving it: make the opponent indifferent

Let Alice hide H with probability p and Bob guess H with probability q. Alice's probability of winning (her expected payoff) is

E_A=p(1-q)+(1-p)q=p(1-2q)+q.

Alice takes q as given and chooses p to maximise E_A:

  • q<\tfrac12: 1-2q>0, E_A rises with p, best is p=1;
  • q>\tfrac12: E_A falls with p, best is p=0;
  • q=\tfrac12: E_A=\tfrac12 whatever p; every p\in[0,1] is optimal.

Likewise Bob's expected payoff is E_B=pq+(1-p)(1-q)=q(2p-1)+1-p, and his best response is q=1 if p>\tfrac12, q=0 if p<\tfrac12, anything if p=\tfrac12.

Definition (mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium). A mixed profile m^* is an equilibrium if for every i, u_i(m_i^*,m_{-i}^*)\ge u_i(m_i,m_{-i}^*) for all mixed strategies m_i of i. With two players and two strategies each, it is a crossing point of the two best-response curves.

The unique equilibrium of matching pennies is (p^*,q^*)=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12): both toss a coin, and each expects \tfrac12.

The key trick. In a mixed equilibrium my probabilities are pinned down by my opponent's payoffs: they must leave the opponent exactly indifferent between his options. Otherwise he would play just one of them, and then I should not be mixing.

4.4 The mixed equilibrium of the Battle of the Sexes

Let Alice go to the ballet with probability p and Bob with probability q.

E_A=2pq+(1-p)(1-q)=p(3q-1)+1-q,\qquad E_B=pq+2(1-p)(1-q)=q(3p-2)+2(1-p).

Alice's best response: p=1 if q>\tfrac13, p=0 if q<\tfrac13. Bob's best response: q=1 if p>\tfrac23, q=0 if p<\tfrac23.

Check directly with "make the opponent indifferent". Bob gets 1\cdot p at the ballet and 2(1-p) at the boxing match; indifference requires p=2(1-p), i.e. p=\tfrac23. Alice gets 2q at the ballet and 1-q at boxing; indifference requires q=\tfrac13.

There are three crossings: (0, 0), i.e. (box, box); (1, 1), i.e. (bal, bal); and the mixed equilibrium (\tfrac23,\tfrac13). In the mixed equilibrium Alice goes to the ballet two times out of three and Bob one time out of three; they can roll a die, with Alice going to the ballet on 1–4 and to boxing on 5–6. The expected payoffs are

E_A=2\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac13+\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac23=\tfrac49+\tfrac29=\tfrac23,\qquad E_B=\tfrac23.

Both expect only \tfrac23, less than the smaller payoff 1 in either pure equilibrium, because with probability \tfrac59 they miss each other.

4.5 The inspection game

Example (Inspection game I: simultaneous moves). A firm can pollute (P) or clean up (Cl). Polluting earns 4; cleaning costs 1 and earns 3. The environmental agency can inspect (I, cost C<5) or trust (T). A polluter caught during an inspection pays a fine F>1. A clean river is worth 5 to the agency.

Firm \ Agency I T
P 4-F, 5-C 4, 0
Cl 3, 5-C 3, 5

(When the firm pollutes and is inspected, pollution is stopped and the agency gets 5-C.) There is no pure equilibrium: the firm pollutes, so the agency wants to inspect, so the firm wants to clean, so the agency wants to trust, so the firm wants to pollute…

Let the firm pollute with probability p and the agency inspect with probability q.

  • Firm indifferent: polluting gives 4-qF, cleaning gives 3; equality gives q^*=\dfrac1F.
  • Agency indifferent: inspecting gives 5-C, trusting gives 5(1-p); equality gives p^*=\dfrac C5.

The equilibrium is (p^*,q^*)=(\tfrac C5,\tfrac1F), with expected payoffs 3 for the firm and 5-C for the agency.

Numbers. F=4, C=2: the agency inspects with probability \tfrac14 and the firm pollutes with probability \tfrac25.

Note a counter-intuitive conclusion: raising the fine F does not reduce the probability of pollution; it only lowers the inspection rate. The pollution probability C/5 depends only on the agency's inspection cost, because it must keep the agency indifferent between inspecting and not.

Inspection game II: the agency announces first. If the agency publicly announces whether it will inspect and the firm then decides, the firm cleans up when told "inspect" and pollutes when told "trust". The agency announces an inspection, the firm cleans up, and the payoffs are (3, 5-C), the same as in the mixed equilibrium, but the probability of pollution is now 0.

Inspection game III: many firms. The agency faces a large population of identical firms and announces that it will inspect a fraction \theta of them. A firm does not pollute if and only if

3\ge 4-\theta F\iff \theta\ge\frac1F.

The agency chooses the smallest \theta=1/F. All firms clean up and the agency gets 5-C/F>5-C. Being able to commit to an inspection rate in advance is much better than randomising on the spot; this is the logic behind random spot checks in practice.

4.6 Does an equilibrium always exist? (Advanced)

In one sentence. Once mixing is allowed, strategy sets become "continuous, without holes" segments or simplices, and expected payoffs are linear in one's own probabilities, so a fixed-point theorem guarantees that the best-response curves cross.

Theorem (existence of Nash equilibrium). If for every player i (i) the strategy set S_i is a nonempty, compact (bounded and closed) and convex subset of a Euclidean space, and (ii) the payoff u_i is continuous and quasi-concave in his own strategy s_i, then the game has at least one Nash equilibrium.

Here convex means that the segment joining any two points of the set stays in the set; quasi-concave means that for every \alpha the set \{s_i:u_i(s_i,s_{-i})\ge\alpha\} is convex. The proof uses Kakutani's fixed-point theorem and is not given here.

Check. In matching pennies with pure strategies only, S_i=\{0,1\} (H as 0, T as 1) is compact but not convex: 0.5 lies between 0 and 1 but not in the set, so the theorem does not apply (and indeed there is no equilibrium). With mixing, the strategy set is the segment \{(m(H),m(T)):m(H)+m(T)=1,\ m\ge0\}, compact and convex; the expected payoff is linear in one's own probabilities, hence continuous and quasi-concave, so the theorem applies and an equilibrium exists.

Corollary. Every finite game (finitely many players and strategies) has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.

5. Continuous strategies: quantity and price competition

Intuition. Firms choosing output or price do not have two or three options but a whole number line. Then a best response is a function, and an equilibrium is a crossing of two best-response curves. In the same market, whether firms compete in prices or quantities, and whether they move at once or in turn, gives wildly different results: anything from the competitive price to nearly the monopoly price.

The whole chapter uses one example:

Benchmark market. Demand Q=a-P (inverse demand P=a-Q), two identical firms, marginal cost = average cost = c. Numerical examples use a=13, c=1.

5.1 Benchmark: monopoly

One firm chooses q to maximise (a-q)q-cq. The first-order condition a-2q-c=0 gives

q_m=\frac{a-c}2,\quad p_m=\frac{a+c}2,\quad \pi_m=\frac{(a-c)^2}4.

Numbers: q_m=6, p_m=7, \pi_m=36.

5.2 The Bertrand model: simultaneous pricing

The two firms set prices p_1,p_2 at the same time. The products are identical, consumers buy only the cheaper one, and at equal prices the market is split in half. Firm 1's demand:

q_1(p_1,p_2)=\begin{cases}0,& p_1>p_2,\\ \dfrac{a-p_1}2,& p_1=p_2,\\ a-p_1,& p_1<p_2.\end{cases}

Proposition. The unique Nash equilibrium is p_1=p_2=c.

In one sentence. As long as the price is above cost, either firm can cut it a tiny bit, take the whole market and nearly double its profit, so the price is pushed all the way down to cost.

Proof. (1) If p_1>p_2, firm 1 sells nothing and can undercut p_2 to take the market, so this is not an equilibrium; symmetrically for p_2>p_1. Hence p_1=p_2=p. (2) If p<c, both lose money and would rather shut down. (3) If p>c, each earns (p-c)\frac{a-p}2. If firm 1 charges p-\varepsilon it takes the whole market and earns (p-\varepsilon-c)(a-p+\varepsilon); for small \varepsilon this is close to (p-c)(a-p), more than half of it, so the deviation pays. (4) Only p=c is left: a higher price sells nothing and a lower price loses money, so nobody deviates. \square

Numbers: p=1, Q=12, both profits 0.

This result is the Bertrand paradox: just two firms, yet the perfectly competitive outcome. It relies on three assumptions: (1) identical products; (2) identical costs; (3) each firm can supply the whole market. Chapter 6 relaxes them one by one.

5.3 The Cournot model: simultaneous quantities

The two firms choose outputs q_1,q_2 at the same time, and the price clears the market: P=a-q_1-q_2.

Firm 1 takes q_2 as given and maximises (a-q_1-q_2)q_1-cq_1. The first-order condition a-2q_1-q_2-c=0 gives the best-response function

q_1=BR_1(q_2)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{a-c-q_2}2,& q_2<a-c,\\ 0,& q_2\ge a-c.\end{cases}

(If the rival produces the competitive output a-c or more, firm 1 shuts down; if the rival produces nothing, firm 1 produces the monopoly output.) Symmetrically q_2=BR_2(q_1).

Finding the crossing. Solve q_1=\frac{a-c-q_2}2, q_2=\frac{a-c-q_1}2. By symmetry guess q_1=q_2=q; then q=\frac{a-c-q}2, so

q_1^*=q_2^*=\frac{a-c}3,\quad Q=\frac{2(a-c)}3,\quad P=\frac{a+2c}3,\quad \pi_i=\frac{(a-c)^2}9.

Numbers: each produces 4, total 8, price 5, each earns (5-1)\times4=16.

The Cournot equilibrium is inefficient (for the firms). If they colluded and split the monopoly output, each would produce 3 at price 7 and earn 18 > 16. But that is not an equilibrium: if the rival produces 3, my best response is BR(3)=\frac{12-3}2=4.5. The price is then 13-7.5=5.5 and I earn 4.5\times4.5=20.25>18. Everyone wants to secretly produce more: a prisoners' dilemma again.

5.4 The Stackelberg model: sequential quantities

Firm 1 (the leader) sets q_1 first; firm 2 (the follower) sees it and then sets q_2. Use backward induction (formally introduced in Chapter 9): solve the last mover's problem first.

The follower's best response is as in Cournot: q_2=\frac{a-c-q_1}2.

The leader knows the follower will react this way, so it maximises

\Big(a-q_1-\frac{a-c-q_1}2\Big)q_1-cq_1=\frac{(a-c-q_1)\,q_1}2.

This has the same shape as the monopoly problem, with solution q_1=\frac{a-c}2. Hence

q_2=\frac{a-c}4,\quad Q=\frac{3(a-c)}4,\quad P=\frac{a+3c}4,\quad \pi_1=\frac{(a-c)^2}8,\quad \pi_2=\frac{(a-c)^2}{16}.

Numbers: q_1=6, q_2=3, P=4, \pi_1=18, \pi_2=9. The leader earns 18, more than the Cournot 16; the follower only 9. In quantity competition moving first is an advantage: the leader grabs a large output and the follower has to give way.

Could the leader threaten "I will produce the competitive output a-c, so entry will not pay"? It can be checked that this would give the leader itself zero profit, worse than 18, so the threat is not credible.

5.5 The four structures compared

Structure Total output Price Profit per firm
Monopoly 6 7 36 (one firm)
Cournot 8 5 16, 16
Stackelberg 9 4 18, 9
Bertrand 12 1 0, 0

The Bertrand result coincides with perfect competition and is Pareto efficient (total surplus is maximal); in the other three the price exceeds marginal cost and there is a deadweight loss.

5.6 Price competition with differentiated products

In reality two dishwasher brands are similar but not identical. Let

q_1=150-p_1+p_2,\qquad q_2=100-p_2+p_1,\qquad \text{cost } c=50.

Raising one's own price lowers sales; the rival raising its price raises them.

Firm 1 maximises (p_1-50)(150-p_1+p_2). The first-order condition 150-2p_1+p_2+50=0 gives

p_1=BR_1(p_2)=100+\frac{p_2}2.

Firm 2 maximises (p_2-50)(100-p_2+p_1), giving p_2=BR_2(p_1)=75+\frac{p_1}2.

Solving the system. Substitute: p_1=100+\frac12\big(75+\frac{p_1}2\big)=137.5+\frac{p_1}4, so \frac34p_1=137.5 and

p_1^*=\frac{550}3\approx183.33,\qquad p_2^*=75+\frac{275}3=\frac{500}3\approx166.67.

Sales are q_1=150-183.33+166.67\approx133.33 and q_2\approx116.67. Profits are \pi_1=(p_1-50)q_1=(400/3)^2\approx17\,778 and \pi_2=(350/3)^2\approx13\,611.

Prices are far above the cost of 50: product differentiation preserves pricing power, and the Bertrand paradox disappears.

5.7 Price leadership

Suppose firm 1 sets its price first and firm 2 follows. Firm 1 anticipates p_2=75+p_1/2 and maximises

(p_1-50)\Big(150-p_1+75+\frac{p_1}2\Big)=(p_1-50)\Big(225-\frac{p_1}2\Big).

The first-order condition 225-p_1+25=0 gives p_1=250, hence p_2=75+125=200. Sales are q_1=150-250+200=100 and q_2=100-200+250=150. Profits are \pi_1=200\times100=20\,000 and \pi_2=150\times150=22\,500.

This time the follower earns more! In price competition moving first is a disadvantage: the leader commits to a high price, and the follower just undercuts it a little to take sales. The exact opposite of Stackelberg, where leading in quantities pays.

5.8 Strategic substitutes and complements

Slope of best response Meaning Example
Strategic substitutes downward the rival does more, I do less Cournot (quantities)
Strategic complements upward the rival does more, I do more too differentiated Bertrand (prices)

This distinction explains whether moving first helps or hurts. With strategic substitutes the leader "does more first" and forces the rival to back off; with strategic complements a leader who "gets tough first" makes the rival tougher too, and it is better to "go soft first". Games with strategic complements (also called supermodular games) matter in industrial organisation and mechanism design; their comparative statics (how equilibria move when parameters change) are especially well behaved.

6. Pricing: escaping the Bertrand paradox

Intuition. The Bertrand model says two firms are enough to push the price down to cost, which does not match reality: airlines, hotels and telecom companies make money. The paradox comes from three assumptions (identical products, identical costs, unlimited capacity). This chapter relaxes them in turn and shows that each one alone is enough to keep prices above cost.

6.1 Hotelling's linear city: spatial differentiation

Consumers are spread uniformly over the interval [0,1]. Firm 1 is at 0, firm 2 at 1, both with marginal cost c. Each consumer buys at most one unit and values it at a; buying also costs a travel cost t per unit of distance. A consumer living at x gets a-p_1-tx from firm 1 and a-p_2-t(1-x) from firm 2. (Assume a>c+t so the whole market is served.)

The products are physically the same but no longer the same for consumers at different places: this is spatial differentiation.

Who buys where? When p_2-t<p_1<p_2+t there is a consumer x^* who is indifferent between the two:

p_1+tx^*=p_2+t(1-x^*)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^*=\frac{p_2-p_1}{2t}+\frac12.

Consumers in [0,x^*) buy from firm 1 and the rest from firm 2, so firm 1's market share is m_1=x^*. (If p_1\ge p_2+t firm 1 sells nothing; if p_1\le p_2-t it takes everything.)

Equilibrium. Firm 1 maximises

\pi_1=(p_1-c)\Big(\frac{p_2-p_1}{2t}+\frac12\Big)=(p_1-c)\frac{p_2+t-p_1}{2t}.

The first-order condition p_2+t+c-2p_1=0 gives p_1=\frac12(p_2+t+c); symmetrically p_2=\frac12(p_1+t+c). Solving,

p_1^*=p_2^*=c+t,\qquad \text{each serves half the market and earns } \frac t2.

Numbers. c=1, t=2: the equilibrium price is 3 and each firm earns (3-1)\times\frac12=1. The higher the travel cost t (the more consumers care about location), the more pricing power the firms have; as t\to0 we return to Bertrand's p=c.

6.2 Asymmetric costs

The products are identical but marginal costs differ: c_1>c_2. Demand is still Q=a-P.

  • If c_1>\frac{a+c_2}2 (firm 1's cost is above firm 2's monopoly price), firm 1 cannot compete at all; firm 2 charges its monopoly price \frac{a+c_2}2 and earns the monopoly profit \frac{(a-c_2)^2}4.
  • If c_1\le\frac{a+c_2}2, firm 2 prices at c_1 (or a hair below), just pushing firm 1 out, and earns (a-c_1)(c_1-c_2)>0.

Numbers. a=10, c_1=4, c_2=2. Firm 2's monopoly price is 6 > 4, so firm 2 prices at 4 (a hair below), sells 6 units and earns (10-4)(4-2)=12.

Advanced detail. Strictly speaking, whether "p_1=p_2=c_1" is an equilibrium depends on the tie rule. If firm 1 is assumed not to enter at zero profit, it is an equilibrium; if firm 1 also gets half the market at a tie, firm 2 always wants to cut a little more, and since there is no "largest price below c_1", no equilibrium exists in the strict sense. In practice prices are in cents and firm 2 just charges c_1-0.01.

6.3 Capacity constraints (Edgeworth)

If firm 1 can produce at most k_1<a-c, then p_1=p_2=c is no longer an equilibrium: if firm 2 raises its price, some consumers cannot get firm 1's cheap goods and have to buy from firm 2, so the price rise pays.

In practice this is natural: telecom companies have limited spectrum, hotels have a limited number of rooms. When a big event is on, the cheap hotels fill up first and the others raise their prices.

Rationing rules. With limited capacity we must say who gets the cheap goods:

  • Efficient rationing: consumers with the highest valuations buy the cheap goods first. After firm 1 sells k_1, firm 2 faces the residual demand q_2=a-k_1-p_2 (the demand curve shifts left by k_1).
  • Proportional rationing: every consumer has the same chance \frac{k_1}{a-p_1} of getting the cheap goods. Firm 2's residual demand is (a-p_2)\frac{a-p_1-k_1}{a-p_1}.

A two-stage model (Advanced). Let marginal cost be 0, each unit of capacity cost 1, and rationing be efficient. The firms first choose capacities (k_1,k_2) at the same time, then set prices at the same time.

Stage 2. If k_i\le a/3, the unique pricing equilibrium is p_1=p_2=a-k_1-k_2: both produce at full capacity and the market just clears. Check: firm 1 cannot sell more by cutting its price; if it raises its price it faces residual demand a-k_2-p_1, whose unconstrained optimal price \frac{a-k_2}2 is no higher than a-k_1-k_2 (because k_1\le a/3 and k_2\le a/3), so the constraint p_1\ge p_2 binds and the best choice is exactly not to change the price.

Stage 1. Anticipating the price a-k_1-k_2, firm i chooses k_i to maximise (a-k_1-k_2-1)k_i. This is the Cournot problem! The solution is k_1=k_2=\frac{a-1}3.

Numbers. a=10: each firm builds capacity 3, the price is 10-6=4, and each earns (4-1)\times3=9.

Conclusion. "Capacity first, then prices" gives the Cournot outcome. This gives the Cournot model a more realistic reading: a firm's "output" is really the capacity it built in advance.

7. Timing games: preemption and attrition

Intuition. Sometimes the question is not "how much" but "when": when to enter a new market, when to leave a declining industry, when to launch a product. At each moment there are only two options, "wait" and "stop", and stopping is irreversible. If moving first is an advantage, players race to preempt, and the race uses up the first-mover advantage; if moving second is an advantage, players wait each other out to see who gives up first.

Setting. At each time t each player chooses "wait" or "stop" (invest, enter, exit…), and stopping is irreversible. The first to stop is the leader with payoff L(t); the later one is the follower with payoff F(t); stopping together gives M(t) each.

7.1 Preemption: the timing of investment

Two firms each have an investment opportunity that raises their profit flow. Let \pi_{n_in_j} be the profit flow given whether the firm itself has invested (n_i\in\{0,1\}) and whether the rival has. Assume

\pi_{10}>\pi_{00},\quad \pi_{11}>\pi_{01},\quad \pi_{10}-\pi_{00}>\pi_{11}-\pi_{01},\quad \pi_{00}>\pi_{01}.

(Investing always helps; investing first helps more; the rival's investment hurts.) The investment cost falls over time, C(t)=ce^{-\mu t}, and the discount rate is r>\mu>0. So there is a trade-off: investing early secures the first-mover advantage, investing late is cheaper.

With roles fixed in advance. If one firm is bound to be the leader, the optimal investment times follow from first-order conditions:

e^{-\mu T_l}=\frac{\pi_{10}-\pi_{00}}{c(r+\mu)},\qquad e^{-\mu T_f}=\frac{\pi_{11}-\pi_{01}}{c(r+\mu)},\qquad e^{-\mu T_s}=\frac{\pi_{11}-\pi_{00}}{c(r+\mu)},

for the leader, the follower and "investing together" respectively. The assumptions give T_l<T_f<T_s.

Without fixed roles. On some interval (t_1,t_2) we have L(t)>F(t)>M(t): both firms want to lead, and investing together is what they fear most.

At each instant in that interval the choice "invest or wait" looks like this:

1 \ 2 invest wait
invest M, M L, F
wait F, L play again next instant

Look for a symmetric mixed equilibrium in which each firm invests with probability p. Making the rival indifferent between "invest" and "wait" gives

p^*=\frac{L(t)-F(t)}{L(t)-M(t)},

and then each firm's expected value is exactly F(t).

Rent equalisation. Before t_1 nobody wants to lead. At t_1, L(t_1)=F(t_1) and the firms are indifferent between leading and following, so one invests at t_1 and the other waits until T_f. The leader gets no first-mover advantage after all: the urge to preempt pulls investment forward to the moment when the advantage is exactly zero. This is called rent equalisation (rent dissipation).

7.2 Product races

Setting. Alice and Bob are both developing a new product and racing to launch. If Alice launches at time t, it succeeds with probability p_1(t) (continuous and increasing, p_1(0)=0, p_1(\infty)=1). If it succeeds she wins the whole market; if it fails, Bob can take as long as he needs to get it right. Bob is similar with p_2(t). If they launch at the same time, Alice wins with probability q_1 and Bob with q_2=1-q_1. Both maximise their probability of winning.

So Alice's winning probability is p_1 as a leader and 1-p_2 as a follower.

Proposition. In equilibrium both launch at the same time t^*, with

p_1(t^*)+p_2(t^*)=1.

In one sentence. Whoever launches early can wait a little to improve the odds; when the "leader's winning chance" equals the "follower's winning chance", nobody wants to move earlier or later.

Proof. Step 1: if Alice launches before Bob, she can wait a little (still before Bob) and improve her success probability, so in equilibrium they launch together, at t^* say. Step 2: if p_1(t^*)>q_1, by continuity Alice still has p_1>q_1 a little earlier and would move earlier; so p_1(t^*)\le q_1, likewise p_2(t^*)\le q_2, and adding gives p_1+p_2\le1. Step 3: if 1-p_2(t^*)>q_1, Alice would rather wait a little and follow; so 1-p_2\le q_1, likewise 1-p_1\le q_2, and adding gives p_1+p_2\ge1. Together, p_1+p_2=1. \square

Example. p_1(t)=t/10, p_2(t)=t/15 (Alice develops faster). From \frac t{10}+\frac t{15}=1 we get t^*=6, where p_1=0.6 and p_2=0.4. At that moment Alice's chance of winning as a leader, 0.6, equals her chance as a follower, 1-0.4=0.6: the first-mover advantage is used up again.

7.3 The war of attrition

Setting. Two identical players fight over a prize worth v>0. Each unit of time spent fighting costs 1. If one gives up, the other wins the prize; if both give up at once, nobody gets it. A real example: two firms in a declining industry are both losing money, and whoever exits first leaves the other as a monopolist.

This game has many equilibria, for example "player 1 never gives up, player 2 gives up at once". Since the players are identical, we look for a symmetric equilibrium.

At any moment (assuming nobody has given up yet) each chooses to fight (F) or stop (S):

1 \ 2 F S
F −1, −1, then play again v, 0
S 0, v 0, 0

Let each fight with probability p. Stopping is worth 0; fighting must be worth the same (otherwise nobody would mix). Fighting means: if the rival stops (probability 1-p) I get v; if the rival fights too (probability p) I pay 1 and am back in the same situation (worth 0). Setting this to 0:

(1-p)v-p=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p^*=\frac v{v+1}.

Example. v=3: at every moment each player keeps fighting with probability \frac34 and gives up with probability \frac14. The probability does not change over time, so this is a stationary mixed equilibrium, and its expected value is 0: the whole value of the prize is burnt in the cost of waiting each other out.

Extensions. If the prize changes over time (for example R&D productivity rises), strategies are no longer stationary. If the players differ (say a large and a small firm), conclusions change too: some models show that in a declining industry the large firm exits first, because it becomes unprofitable earlier; but if the large firm can shed part of its capacity, that result fails.

8. Information structure: extensive form and Bayesian games

Intuition. Matrices suit simultaneous moves, but many games have an order of moves: some players see others' actions, some do not, and some hold information others lack. This chapter shows how to draw "who knows what, and when" with a game tree, and how, when opponents have private information, to update beliefs with Bayes' rule and define equilibrium.

8.1 Sequential moves change what a strategy is

Back to DVD/Blu-ray, but now Alice chooses first and Bob sees her choice before choosing. Alice still has two strategies, but Bob's strategy is now a complete contingent plan that says what he does after each of Alice's choices. He has 4 strategies:

Notation Meaning
(D|D; B|B) follow: I choose what she chose
(B|D; D|B) do the opposite
(D|D; D|B) always DVD
(B|D; B|B) always Blu-ray

("B|D" reads "if Alice chooses D, I choose B".) The normal form:

Alice \ Bob (D|D; B|B) (B|D; D|B) (D|D; D|B) (B|D; B|B)
DVD 1, 1 −1, −1 1, 1 −1, −1
Blu-ray 3, 3 −1, −1 −1, −1 3, 3

There are 3 Nash equilibria: (Blu-ray, follow) and (Blu-ray, always Blu-ray), both with (3, 3), and (DVD, always DVD) with (1, 1). The third one is odd: Bob "threatens" to choose DVD even if Alice chooses Blu-ray. This is exactly the kind of "non-credible threat" Chapter 9 will rule out.

8.2 Game trees

The extensive form is the most complete description of a game: who moves, when, knowing what, and with which options. It is drawn as a game tree:

  • Nodes: points where some player (or "nature") moves, or where the game ends.
  • Branches: actions, each leading from one node to the next.
  • The initial node (root) has no predecessor; terminal nodes have no successor and carry everyone's payoffs.
  • A path is a sequence of nodes and branches from the root to a terminal node.

A finite extensive-form game consists of: the set of players plus "nature" (player 0, standing for chance); a tree with no loops; an assignment of each nonterminal node to a player; the probabilities nature uses at its nodes; the information sets; and the payoffs at each terminal node.

8.3 Information sets

Definition. An information set of player i is a set of his decision nodes such that, when it is his turn, he knows he is at one of these nodes but cannot tell which. So the same actions must be available at all nodes of an information set, and none of them precedes another. Every node belongs to exactly one information set.

In pictures, nodes of the same information set are joined by a dashed line.

On the left Bob cannot see Alice's choice, which is the same as moving at the same time (whether Alice moves "first" does not matter); on the right he can.

Information classes:

Name Meaning
perfect information every information set is a single node: you know everything that has happened when you move
imperfect information some information set contains several nodes
common knowledge everyone knows it, everyone knows that everyone knows it, … forever
game of certainty nature does not move after any player has moved
symmetric information when moving or at the end, nobody knows less than anyone else
incomplete information nature moves first and at least one player does not see its choice

Game-theoretic models always assume that the information structure itself is common knowledge: everyone knows how precise the others' information is, though he may not know which node has been reached. A game of incomplete information is always also a game of imperfect information.

8.4 Bayesian games

Harsanyi's trick. "I do not know your payoffs" sounds hard to model. Harsanyi's idea: suppose nature first draws each player's "type" (payoffs, information and so on) at random, each player sees only his own type, and the distribution of the draw is common knowledge. Then "not knowing who you are facing" becomes "not knowing what nature drew", which can be handled with probabilities.

Definition (Bayesian game). A Bayesian game consists of \{(A_i,T_i,\mu_i,u_i)\}_{i=1}^n: A_i is the action set, T_i the set of types, \mu_i(\cdot\mid t_i) is i's belief about the others' types when his own type is t_i, and u_i(a,t) is the payoff.

A strategy is a function from types to actions, s_i:T_i\to A_i: for each type one might be, it says what to do.

Definition (Bayesian Nash equilibrium). A profile s^* is a Bayesian Nash equilibrium if for every i and every type t_i

E_{t_{-i}}\big[u_i(s_i^*(t_i),s_{-i}^*(t_{-i}),t)\big]\ge E_{t_{-i}}\big[u_i(a_i,s_{-i}^*(t_{-i}),t)\big]\quad\text{for all } a_i\in A_i,

with expectations taken under \mu_i(\cdot\mid t_i). That is, every type best-responds (in expectation) to the others' strategies.

8.5 Bayes' rule and the three-step check

As the game unfolds, players observe others' actions and update their beliefs. Bayes' rule:

P(\text{state } k\mid\text{observed } B)=\frac{P(B\mid k)\,P(k)}{\sum_jP(B\mid j)\,P(j)}.

The catch is that P(B\mid k) (the probability that the other chooses B in state k) depends on the other's equilibrium strategy, so beliefs cannot be computed apart from the equilibrium. Checking a candidate equilibrium takes three steps:

  1. Propose a strategy profile;
  2. Compute the beliefs it generates (with Bayes' rule);
  3. Check that, given these beliefs, everyone's strategy is a best response.

Example (DVD/Blu-ray with unknown payoffs). Alice first chooses B (Blu-ray) or D (DVD), and Bob sees it before choosing. Bob is unsure which payoff case applies; his prior is 0.6, 0.3, 0.1. Alice knows the true case. Payoffs (Alice, Bob):

Case (prob.) (B,B) (B,D) (D,B) (D,D)
1 (0.6) 3, 3 −1, −1 −1, −1 1, 1
2 (0.3) 2, 2 −1, −1 −1, −1 4, 4
3 (0.1) 4, 2 0, 1 −1, −1 1, 2

Step 1, candidate: Alice chooses B in cases 1 and 3 and D in case 2; Bob follows Alice.

Step 2, beliefs: after seeing B, P(B\mid1)=1, P(B\mid2)=0, P(B\mid3)=1, so P(B)=0.6+0.1=0.7 and

P(1\mid B)=\frac{0.6}{0.7}=\frac67,\quad P(2\mid B)=0,\quad P(3\mid B)=\frac17.

After seeing D, P(D)=0.3 and P(2\mid D)=1.

Step 3, check Bob: after B, choosing B gives \frac67\cdot3+\frac17\cdot2=\frac{20}7 and choosing D gives \frac67\cdot(-1)+\frac17\cdot1=-\frac57, so B is better. After D (surely case 2), choosing D gives 4 > choosing B gives −1. So "follow" is a best response.

Check Alice: since Bob follows, Alice compares 3 (B) and 1 (D) in case 1 and chooses B; 2 and 4 in case 2 and chooses D; 4 and 1 in case 3 and chooses B. This matches the candidate.

So this is a Bayesian Nash equilibrium.

9. Dynamic games: subgame perfection and backward induction

Intuition. In sequential games a Nash equilibrium can be propped up by a non-credible threat: "if you come in, I will destroy us both." When the moment actually comes, the threatener would not do it. Subgame perfect equilibrium requires everyone to act optimally in every part of the game; for games of perfect information it is found by backward induction, working from the last move back to the first.

9.1 Nash equilibria of sequential games

A sequential game can also be written in normal form (each strategy is a complete plan), and its Nash equilibria are defined as before: given the others' strategies, nobody gains by switching his own strategy.

Example. Player 1 chooses L or R at A. L leads to B, where player 2 chooses L′ (payoffs (2, 1)) or R′ ((0, 3)); R leads to C, where player 2 chooses L′ ((4, 1)) or R′ ((1, 0)).

Write player 2's strategies as {choice at B, choice at C}:

1 \ 2 {L′, L′} {L′, R′} {R′, L′} {R′, R′}
L 2, 1 2, 1 0, 3 0, 3
R 4, 1 1, 0 4, 1 1, 0

Nash equilibria: (R, {L′, L′}) and (R, {R′, L′}), both following the path A→C→(4, 1).

9.2 Subgames and subgame perfect equilibrium

Definition (subgame). A subgame is a branch of the original tree that (1) starts at a single-node information set and contains all nodes after it; (2) does not cut any information set (each information set is either entirely inside the branch or entirely outside); (3) keeps the original terminal payoffs. The whole game is itself a subgame (the trivial one); the others are proper subgames.

The example above has 3 subgames, starting at A, B and C.

Definition (subgame perfect equilibrium, SPE). A strategy profile is a subgame perfect equilibrium if it is a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.

Example (removing a non-credible threat). Player 1 chooses L or R at O. L leads to A, where player 2 chooses L′ ((1, 1)) or R′ ((0, 1)). R leads to B, where player 2 chooses L′ or R′, and then player 1 chooses L″ or R″ without seeing player 2's choice (her two nodes form one information set). Payoffs after B:

1 \ 2 L′ R′
L″ 2, 2 0, 2
R″ 0, 1 1, 0

The unique Nash equilibrium of this subgame is (L″, L′) with (2, 2): given L′, player 1 gets 2 > 0 from L″; given L″, player 2 gets 2 from either L′ or R′, so L′ is fine; in every other cell someone wants to switch. In the subgame starting at A, player 2 gets 1 from L′ or R′, so either is fine.

The whole game also has Nash equilibria that prescribe (R″, R′) in the B subgame, for example "player 1 goes L at the root; if B were reached, player 1 would choose R″ and player 2 R′". B is never reached in such an equilibrium, so these prescriptions do not affect anyone's payoff. But (R″, R′) is not a Nash equilibrium of the B subgame: given that player 1 chooses R″, player 2 gets 1 from L′ but 0 from R′. Player 2's R′ at B is a non-credible threat, and such an equilibrium is not subgame perfect. SPE requires (L″, L′) in the B subgame; player 1 at the root then compares 2 from R with at most 1 from L and chooses R, with payoffs (2, 2).

Key point. A Nash equilibrium that is not subgame perfect relies on non-credible behaviour off the equilibrium path: those nodes are never reached in equilibrium, so "talking tough costs nothing". Subgame perfection requires every threat to be one the player would actually carry out when the moment comes.

9.3 Backward induction and Kuhn's theorem

Theorem (Kuhn). Every finite sequential game of perfect information has a subgame perfect equilibrium, and all its subgame perfect equilibria can be found by backward induction.

Backward induction, step by step:

  1. Find all nodes whose successors are all terminal;
  2. At each such node let the mover pick his best branch, and replace the node by the resulting payoffs ("pruning");
  3. Treat these nodes as new terminal nodes and repeat until the root is reached.

In the example of 9.1: at B player 2 chooses R′ (3 > 1), at C he chooses L′ (1 > 0); after pruning, player 1 compares 0 from L and 4 from R and chooses R. The SPE is (R, {R′, L′}). Note that the other Nash equilibrium of 9.1, (R, {L′, L′}), is not subgame perfect: choosing L′ at B is not optimal.

9.4 Application 1: the takeover game

An investor considers taking over a firm. The shares are worth 100 now and would be worth 110 after the takeover. The investor bids b per share; the firm can accept (selling at b to the investor) or reject (buying the shares back at b). Payoffs:

  • No bid: (0, 0).
  • Bid accepted: investor 110-b, firm b-100.
  • Bid rejected: investor 0, firm 100-b.

Backward induction. The firm accepts if and only if b-100\ge100-b, i.e. b\ge100 (assuming it accepts when indifferent). The investor knows this: a bid below 100 is rejected, the same as not bidding; a bid b\ge100 gives 110-b, which falls with b, so she bids b=100 and gains 10 per share.

SPE: the investor bids 100 and the firm accepts. In practice the investor bids a little above 100 so the firm does not hesitate.

9.5 Application 2: the centipede game

From right to left: at the last node player 2 stops and gets 4 (going on gives only 3); at the second-to-last node player 1 stops and gets 4 (going on, the rival would stop and she would get 2); before that player 2 stops and gets 3 (going on gives only 2); at the first node player 1 stops and gets 1 (going on gives only 0).

So the SPE is everyone stops at every node; the game ends at the first move with (1, 0). Yet if both went on to the third node they would get (4, 2), better than (1, 0) for both. As in the prisoners' dilemma, backward induction here predicts something "unreasonable", and in experiments people usually go on for several steps.

9.6 Application 3: the monitoring game

An employer can monitor (M, cost m) or not (NM). The worker knows whether he is monitored and chooses high effort h (cost e) or low effort l. When monitoring, the employer sees effort and pays w_h=30 for high and w_l=10 for low; without monitoring she cannot see it and decides afterwards which wage to pay. The project is worth 90 with high effort and 30 with low effort. Assume 0<m<20 and 0<e<10.

Backward induction. The no-monitoring subgame (the employer picks the wage without seeing effort):

Employer \ Worker h l
w_h 60, 30-e 0, 30
w_l 80, 10-e 20, 10

w_l is dominant for the employer (80>60, 20>0); anticipating it, the worker chooses l (10 > 10-e). Subgame equilibrium (w_l, l), the employer gets 20.

The monitoring subgame: the worker gets 30-e from h and 10 from l, and since e<10 chooses h; the employer gets 90-30-m=60-m.

At the start the employer compares 60-m with 20 and, since m<20, monitors. The unique SPE: the employer monitors (and would pay the low wage without monitoring); the worker exerts high effort when monitored and low effort otherwise. Equilibrium path: monitor → high effort. The normal form has two more Nash equilibria (for example "do not monitor + pay low" with "always low effort"), but they fail to be equilibria in some subgame and are ruled out.

9.7 Behaviour strategies (Advanced)

Example. Player 1 first chooses L or R. After L, player 2 chooses L′ ((1, 1)) or R′ ((0, 0)). After R comes a "matching pennies" subgame: player 2 chooses L′ or R′, and player 1, without seeing it, chooses L″ or R″, with payoffs (3, 0), (0, 3), (0, 3), (3, 0) (player 1 wins on a match).

This subgame has no pure equilibrium; its unique equilibrium has both mixing \frac12–\frac12, with expected payoffs (1.5, 1.5). So the whole game has no pure-strategy SPE.

A behaviour strategy assigns a probability distribution over actions separately at each information set (whereas a mixed strategy randomises over whole plans). The SPE in behaviour strategies is: player 1 chooses R at the root and mixes (0.5, 0.5) in the subgame; player 2 chooses L′ after L and mixes (0.5, 0.5) in the subgame. At the root player 1 compares 1.5 from R and 1 from L and chooses R.

Behaviour versus mixed strategies. For any behaviour strategy there is a mixed strategy that gives the same distribution over terminal nodes. The converse also holds in games with perfect recall (another theorem of Kuhn). Perfect recall means everyone remembers the choices he made at earlier information sets. A counterexample: player 1 first chooses L or R and later reaches an information set with two nodes that correspond exactly to her own earlier choices; she has "forgotten" what she just did.

10. Repeated games: how cooperation is sustained

Intuition. The prisoners' dilemma shows that cooperation is hard to sustain in a one-shot interaction. But firms, neighbours and countries deal with each other again and again. Betraying today gains a little, but invites retaliation tomorrow. If the future matters enough, the threat of "tit for tat" can make cooperation an equilibrium. This chapter shows that finitely many repetitions are often not enough, while infinite repetition (or not knowing when it ends) really can sustain cooperation, and the set of sustainable outcomes is astonishingly large (the folk theorem).

10.1 Basic structure

The same stage game G is played for T periods, and after each period everyone sees the outcome. T finite gives a finitely repeated game, T=\infty an infinitely repeated game.

  • History h^t=(s^1,\dots,s^t): the strategy profiles of all periods up to t. At the start of period 1 the history is empty.
  • Strategy \sigma_i: for each possible history, what to do next period.
  • Payoff: without discounting the sum \sum_tu_i(s^t); with discount factor \delta=\frac1{1+r}, \sum_t\delta^{t-1}u_i(s^t). The closer \delta is to 1, the more patient the players.

10.2 Discounting matters

Example. The stage game below is played twice.

1 \ 2 L R
U 5, 5 0, 6
D 6, 0 2, 2

(D and R are dominant: this is a prisoners' dilemma.) Consider the strategies: both play (D, R) in period 1; in period 2, each cooperates (U or L) if the other "cooperated" in period 1, and otherwise does not. The path is (D, R), (D, R), each getting 2+2\delta.

Checking deviations: player 1's best deviation is to play U in period 1 (getting 0); in period 2 the rival "rewards" her with L by the rule, and she plays D, getting 6, for a total of 6\delta. Not deviating gives 2+2\delta. (Player 2 is symmetric.) So this is a Nash equilibrium when 6\delta\le2+2\delta, i.e. \delta\le\frac12, and not when \delta>\frac12. Whether the same profile is an equilibrium depends on how much the players value the future.

10.3 Finite repetition

Theorem. If s^* is a Nash equilibrium of the stage game, then "play s^* every period" is a Nash equilibrium of the repeated game, and also subgame perfect.

In one sentence. If the others play the stage equilibrium every period regardless of what you do, your best choice each period is simply your best response in the stage game.

Theorem. In any Nash equilibrium of a finitely repeated game, the last period is a Nash equilibrium of the stage game. (The last period has no future, so everyone looks only at that period.)

One-shot deviation principle. A strategy profile is subgame perfect if and only if nobody can gain by deviating in a single period and conforming afterwards. This makes checking SPE easy: instead of all possible complicated deviations, just check "deviate once".

Theorem (unique stage equilibrium ⇒ no cooperation). If the stage game has a unique Nash equilibrium s^*, every finitely repeated game has a unique SPE: play s^* every period.

In one sentence. The last period must be s^*; since the last period's outcome does not depend on earlier play, the second-to-last period has no reason for cooperation either, and so on back to period 1.

Example. A prisoners' dilemma (both defect (0, 0), lone defector 2 against −1, both cooperate (1, 1)) played 10 times: the unique SPE is to defect every period.

With two stage equilibria cooperation is possible. Two firms choose a high (H), medium (M) or low (L) price:

1 \ 2 H M L
H 8, 8 4, 10 0, 4
M 10, 4 6, 6 1, 3
L 4, 0 3, 1 2, 2

The stage game has two equilibria: (M, M) with (6, 6) and (L, L) with (2, 2). (H, H) with (8, 8) is better but not an equilibrium.

Play it twice and consider: both choose H in period 1; if period 1 was (H, H), both choose M in period 2 (reward); otherwise both choose L in period 2 (punishment).

  • Period 2 is always a stage equilibrium, so nobody deviates there.
  • In period 1, conforming gives 8+6\delta; deviating to M gives 10+2\delta. Conforming is better if and only if 10+2\delta\le8+6\delta, i.e. \delta\ge\frac12.

The punishment is credible because the "punishment" (L, L) is itself an equilibrium; it is effective because the gap between the two equilibrium payoffs (6−2=4, times \delta) exceeds the one-time gain from deviating (10−8=2).

10.4 Infinite repetition: grim trigger

Example (infinitely repeated prisoners' dilemma). The same prisoners' dilemma (both cooperate 1 each, lone defector 2 against −1, both defect 0). The grim trigger strategy: cooperate in period 1; keep cooperating as long as nobody has ever defected; once someone defects, defect forever.

There are only two kinds of subgames:

(i) Nobody has defected yet. Cooperating forever gives

1+\delta+\delta^2+\dots=\frac1{1-\delta}.

Deviating in some period (and then defecting forever, as the strategy says, with the rival also defecting forever) gives 2+0+0+\dots=2 from that period on. Payoffs before the deviation are the same either way, so compare only from the deviation onwards:

\frac1{1-\delta}\ge2\iff\delta\ge\frac12.

(ii) Someone has defected. Then both defect forever, 0 per period; switching alone to cooperation only gives −1. No deviation.

So for \delta\ge\frac12 grim trigger is an SPE and cooperation is sustained. Unlike finite repetition, there is no last period, so the chain of backward reasoning never gets started.

Example (a Cournot cartel). Use the benchmark market of Chapter 5 (a=13, c=1). Under collusion each firm produces 3 and earns 18; in the Cournot equilibrium each produces 4 and earns 16. Grim trigger: produce 3 forever; once anyone deviates, return to the Cournot output 4 forever.

  • Conform: \frac{18}{1-\delta}.
  • Deviate once: the best output against a rival producing 3 is 4.5, the price is 5.5, and this period gives 4.5\times4.5=20.25; every later period gives 16. In total 20.25+\frac{16\delta}{1-\delta}.

Conforming is better if and only if

\frac{18}{1-\delta}\ge20.25+\frac{16\delta}{1-\delta}\iff18\ge20.25-4.25\delta\iff\delta\ge\frac{2.25}{4.25}=\frac9{17}\approx0.53.

In general (any a,c) the threshold is the same \frac9{17}: the collusive profit \frac{(a-c)^2}8, the deviation profit \frac{9(a-c)^2}{64} and the Cournot profit \frac{(a-c)^2}9 are all proportional to (a-c)^2.

Even without a pure stage equilibrium. The stage game (U,L)=(3,3), (U,R)=(1,2), (D,L)=(4,0), (D,R)=(0,1) has no pure equilibrium. But "play (U, L) forever; once the other deviates, punish forever (player 1 switches to D, player 2 to R)" is a Nash equilibrium for \delta\ge\frac13: player 2 already gets the highest possible 3 in (U, L) and does not deviate; player 1 deviating to D gets 4+\frac\delta{1-\delta} against \frac3{1-\delta} from conforming, which gives \delta\ge\frac13.

But it is not subgame perfect: suppose (D, R) occurred in period 1. The strategies then prescribe (D, R) forever, giving player 1 zero each period; she could instead play U forever and get \frac\delta{1-\delta}>0. The punishment hurts the punisher herself and so is not credible.

10.5 The folk theorem

Minmax value. Player i's minmax value

r_i=\min_{s_{-i}}\max_{s_i}u_i(s_i,s_{-i})

is the lowest payoff he can guarantee himself when the others gang up to push him down and he defends himself as well as he can. In the example above, player 1 gets at most 4 if the rival plays L and at most 1 if R, so r_1=1; player 2 gets at most 3 if the rival plays U and at most 1 if D, so r_2=1.

  • A payoff vector v is individually rational if v_i\ge r_i for everyone (strictly individually rational: v_i>r_i). Nobody accepts less than he can guarantee himself.
  • The feasible set F is the convex hull of the stage game's payoff vectors: by rotating between outcomes in suitable proportions, the average payoff can be any point in it.

Intuitive argument. To give everyone a strictly individually rational payoff v_i forever, prescribe: keep playing the strategies that generate v; whoever deviates is punished forever by the others with the minmax strategy. If i's best one-time deviation gives A_i, he does not deviate if and only if

\frac{v_i}{1-\delta}\ge A_i+\frac{\delta r_i}{1-\delta}\iff\delta\ge\frac{A_i-v_i}{A_i-r_i}.

Because v_i>r_i the right-hand side is less than 1, so with \delta close enough to 1 nobody wants to deviate.

Example (taking turns). In the example above, the players alternate (U, L) and (D, R), starting with (U, L). Player 1 gets \frac{3}{1-\delta^2} and player 2 gets \frac{3+\delta}{1-\delta^2}. A deviation is punished by (U, R) forever. Player 2 never wants to deviate; player 1 deviating to D in a (U, L) period gets 4+\frac\delta{1-\delta}. Not deviating requires

\frac3{1-\delta^2}\ge4+\frac\delta{1-\delta}\iff3\delta^2-\delta-1\ge0\iff\delta\ge\frac{1+\sqrt{13}}6\approx0.768.

Player 1 deviating to U in a (D, R) period gets 1 every period from then on, \frac1{1-\delta} in total; conforming gives, from that period on, 0+3\delta+0+3\delta^3+\dots=\frac{3\delta}{1-\delta^2}. Not deviating requires 3\delta\ge1+\delta, i.e. \delta\ge\frac12, which is weaker than 0.768.

This equilibrium is again not subgame perfect: player 2 threatens to play R forever to push player 1 down, but as soon as player 1 plays U, player 2 wants to switch back to L. To get a subgame perfect version the punishment must not last forever: after some periods of punishment play returns to cooperation, and whoever carried out the punishment gets a small extra reward, so the punishers are willing to carry it out.

Theorem (folk theorem). Suppose the dimension of the feasible set F equals the number of players. Then for every strictly individually rational feasible payoff v there is \underline\delta<1 such that for all \delta>\underline\delta the infinitely repeated game has a subgame perfect equilibrium with average payoff v.

What it means. Patient players in a long relationship can sustain almost any "reasonable" outcome. The good news is that cooperation is possible; the bad news is that the theory predicts less, because there are so many equilibria.

10.6 Carrot and stick

Example. Stage game:

1 \ 2 L R
U 4, 4 2, 5
D 5, 1 1, 2

Strategies: (U, L) in period 1. Afterwards, if last period was (U, L) or (D, R), play (U, L) this period; otherwise play (D, R) this period. In other words a deviation triggers one period of punishment (D, R) (the stick), and once the punishment has been accepted play returns to (U, L) (the carrot).

Player 1. Conforming gives \frac4{1-\delta}.

  • Deviating to D in a (U, L) period: 5 now, 1 in the punishment period, then back to 4. Not deviating requires 5+\delta+\frac{4\delta^2}{1-\delta}\le\frac4{1-\delta}, which simplifies to 5+\delta\le4+4\delta, i.e. \delta\ge\frac13.
  • Deviating to U in a punishment (D, R) period: 2 now (instead of 1), but the punishment is repeated next period. This simplifies to 2+\delta\le1+4\delta, i.e. \delta\ge\frac13.

Player 2. Deviating to R in a (U, L) period: 5 now, 2 next period in (D, R). Requires 5+2\delta\le4+4\delta, i.e. \delta\ge\frac12. Deviating in a punishment period only lowers his payoff from 2 to 1 and prolongs the punishment, so it does not pay.

So for \delta\ge\frac12 this is an SPE. The punishment lasts one period and is credible: during the punishment the punished player gets only 1, but resisting extends the punishment by another period; the punishing player gets 2 in (D, R) anyway. During the punishment everyone cooperates with it, because accepting the punishment is the only way back to cooperation.

11. Auctions and mechanism design

Intuition. Auctions are one of game theory's greatest successes: spectrum auctions have raised huge sums for governments. In an auction each bidder knows her own value but not the others': a textbook game of private information. This chapter computes optimal bids in various auctions and then reaches a striking result: under certain conditions every auction gives the seller exactly the same expected revenue. Finally the "revelation principle": when designing rules, it is enough to consider rules under which people tell the truth.

11.1 Kinds of auctions

Auction Rule Typical use
posted price a price is posted; take it or leave it retail
first-price sealed bid sealed bids; highest bid wins and pays its own bid government tenders
second-price sealed bid (Vickrey) highest bid wins and pays the second-highest bid sale of public assets
English (ascending) the price rises until only one bidder is left art
Dutch (descending) the price falls from a high level; the first to call stop wins flowers
all-pay everyone pays his highest bid lobbying, contests

Private values: each bidder's value is known only to herself and does not change during the auction. Common value: the item is worth the same to everyone (such as the oil in an offshore tract), but estimates differ. In common-value auctions the winner is prone to the winner's curse: winning means your estimate was the most optimistic of all, and probably too high.

Below: a single item, private values, and a seller who accepts any non-negative price.

11.2 English and second-price auctions: bid your value

English auction. A bidder with value v_i would be foolish to keep her hand up once the price exceeds v_i: winning would lose money. Dropping out while the price is below v_i throws away a chance. So the best strategy is to stay in until the price reaches one's value. The auction ends when the price reaches the second-highest value: the highest-value bidder wins and pays the second-highest value.

Theorem. In a second-price sealed-bid auction, bidding one's value b_i=v_i weakly dominates every other bid.

In one sentence. Your bid only decides whether you win, not what you pay (you pay someone else's bid); bidding your value makes you win exactly when winning is profitable and lose exactly when winning would cost you.

Proof. Let B=\max_{j\ne i}b_j be the highest of the other bids. Bidding the value, if v_i>B she wins v_i-B>0, and if v_i<B she loses and gets 0 (at a tie she shares, still a non-negative payoff).

  • Bidding low, b_i<v_i: the outcome is the same when B<b_i or B>v_i; when b_i<B<v_i she loses a deal that would have earned v_i-B>0. Never better, sometimes worse.
  • Bidding high, b_i>v_i: the outcome is the same when B<v_i or B>b_i; when v_i<B<b_i she wins but pays B>v_i and loses money. Never better, sometimes worse. \square

Example. Three bidders with values 10, 7 and 4 all bid their values. The bidder with value 10 wins, pays 7 and gains 3. If she bid 6 instead she would lose to the bid of 7 and get nothing; if the bidder with value 7 bid 12 she would win but pay 10 and lose 3.

English and second-price auctions are equivalent: the winner is the highest-value bidder and pays the second-highest value in both.

11.3 First-price auctions: shade your bid

Two risk-neutral bidders, with values independent and uniform on [0,1]. The highest bid wins and pays its own bid; ties are broken by a coin toss.

Why shade? Bidding one's value would earn 0 even when winning. Bidding a bit lower lowers the chance of winning but makes winning profitable.

Finding the equilibrium. Guess that the rival bids linearly, b_j(v_j)=\beta v_j. If I bid b my chance of winning is

P(\beta v_j<b)=P\Big(v_j<\frac b\beta\Big)=\frac b\beta\quad(b\le\beta).

I maximise (v_i-b)\frac b\beta; the first-order condition v_i-2b=0 gives b=\frac{v_i}2. So \beta=\frac12 is consistent:

b^*(v)=\frac v2.

A more general derivation (Advanced). Let the symmetric equilibrium strategy b(\cdot) be strictly increasing and differentiable. Bidding b wins with probability P(b(v_j)<b)=b^{-1}(b). Maximising (v_i-b)\,b^{-1}(b), the first-order condition at equilibrium (b=b(v_i)) becomes

b'(v)\,v+b(v)=v\iff\frac{d}{dv}\big(v\,b(v)\big)=v\iff v\,b(v)=\frac{v^2}2+C.

A bidder with value 0 bids 0, so C=0 and b(v)=\frac v2. With n bidders the same method gives b(v)=\frac{n-1}nv: the more bidders, the fiercer the competition and the less shading.

The Dutch auction is equivalent to the first-price auction: the moment you call stop is your sealed bid, and the winner pays the price she "bid".

11.4 The revenue equivalence theorem

Example (two bidders, values uniform on [0,1]).

First price. The winner pays \frac12\max(v_1,v_2). Let z=\max(v_1,v_2); P(z\le x)=P(v_1\le x)P(v_2\le x)=x^2, with density 2x, so

E[z]=\int_0^1x\cdot2x\,dx=\frac23,\qquad\text{seller's expected revenue}=\frac12\cdot\frac23=\frac13.

Second price. The winner pays \min(v_1,v_2). Since \min+\max=v_1+v_2, E[\min]=1-\frac23=\frac13.

Exactly the same! And since English ≈ second price and Dutch ≈ first price, all four auctions give the seller an expected revenue of \frac13.

Theorem (revenue equivalence). In a symmetric independent-private-values sealed-bid auction (n risk-neutral bidders, identically distributed values with a continuous positive density), suppose the symmetric equilibrium is strictly increasing and (a) the bidder with the highest value wins, and (b) a bidder with value 0 expects to pay 0. Then:

  1. The expected payment of a bidder with value v does not depend on the auction format, only on the distribution of the others' values;
  2. hence the seller's expected revenue does not depend on the auction format.

Condition (a) is the efficiency condition: the item goes to whoever values it most.

11.5 The double auction

One buyer, one seller, one item. The seller's value v_s and the buyer's value v_b are private, independent and uniform on [0,1]. They simultaneously name prices, p_s (the seller's ask) and p_b (the buyer's bid). If p_b\ge p_s they trade at the midpoint \frac{p_s+p_b}2; otherwise there is no trade.

This game has many equilibria; we look for a linear equilibrium. Let p_s=\alpha_s+\beta_sv_s and p_b=\alpha_b+\beta_bv_b.

Buyer. The seller's ask is uniform on [\alpha_s,\alpha_s+\beta_s]. Bidding p_b, the buyer trades with probability \frac{p_b-\alpha_s}{\beta_s}, and given trade the expected ask is \frac{\alpha_s+p_b}2, so she maximises

\Big(v_b-\frac{p_b+\frac{\alpha_s+p_b}2}2\Big)\frac{p_b-\alpha_s}{\beta_s}.

The first-order condition gives p_b=\frac23v_b+\frac13\alpha_s.

Seller. Symmetrically, p_s=\frac23v_s+\frac13(\alpha_b+\beta_b).

Putting them together. \beta_b=\beta_s=\frac23, \alpha_b=\frac{\alpha_s}3, \alpha_s=\frac{\alpha_b+2/3}3. Solving gives \alpha_s=\frac14 and \alpha_b=\frac1{12}:

p_b(v_b)=\frac1{12}+\frac23v_b,\qquad p_s(v_s)=\frac14+\frac23v_s.

The trade condition p_b\ge p_s becomes v_b\ge v_s+\frac14.

Example. v_b=0.8, v_s=0.3: the buyer bids \frac1{12}+0.533=0.617, the seller asks 0.25+0.2=0.45, and they trade at 0.533. If v_b=0.5 and v_s=0.3: p_b=0.417<p_s=0.45, no trade, even though the buyer values the item more than the seller and trade would benefit both.

Buyers with v_b<\frac14 and sellers with v_s>\frac34 never trade. Myerson and Satterthwaite (1983) showed that, with uniform values, this linear equilibrium gives both sides higher expected payoffs than any other Bayesian Nash equilibrium: the efficiency loss caused by private information cannot be fully removed.

11.6 Mechanism design and the revelation principle

The question. Can we design selling rules that achieve the outcome we want?

Definition (selling mechanism). A selling mechanism specifies the set \Theta_i of messages each buyer may send; given all messages \theta, the probability q_i(\theta) that buyer i gets the item (summing to at most 1); and the payment \tau_i(\theta) he makes.

Every sealed-bid auction is a selling mechanism. In the first-price auction, for example, the message is the bid; the highest bidder (each of k tied bidders with probability \frac1k) gets the item and pays his own bid. The second-price auction is the same except that the winner pays the highest of the other bids. A buyer's payoff is q_i(\theta)v_i-\tau_i(\theta).

In a direct mechanism the message is "report your value", \Theta_i=V_i. A direct mechanism is incentive compatible if everyone reporting truthfully is an equilibrium.
