Theorem (revelation principle, Myerson 1979). For any selling mechanism and any of its equilibria there is a direct, incentive-compatible mechanism with exactly the same allocation and payments.

In one sentence. Let the mechanism play your old equilibrium strategy for you: you just report your true value, and the mechanism computes the bid you would have made and applies the old rules; since the old strategy was optimal for you, telling the truth is optimal too.

Why it matters. The designer need not search through infinitely many complicated rules; it is enough to consider direct mechanisms in which people tell the truth. The second-price auction is a ready example: it is itself direct and incentive compatible.

12. Dynamic games of incomplete information: perfect Bayesian equilibrium and signalling

Intuition. When the informed side moves first and the uninformed side moves after watching, the action itself carries information: a used-car seller's asking price or a job applicant's education may reveal their "type". Such games often have no proper subgames, so subgame perfection loses its bite. The new tool is perfect Bayesian equilibrium: everyone holds a belief about what he cannot see, beliefs must be consistent with strategies (using Bayes' rule wherever possible), and actions must be optimal given beliefs.

12.1 The market for lemons: a game without subgames

Used cars come in high quality (h) and low quality (l, "lemons"), half each. The seller knows the quality; the buyer does not. The seller's reservation prices are s_h>s_l; the buyer's reservation prices satisfy b_h>s_h>b_l>s_l.

If the buyer also knew the quality (complete information), the seller would ask b_h for a good car and b_l for a bad one, and both would sell.

With asymmetric information. Simplify: the seller can only ask s_h or s_l. The buyer sees the price and decides whether to buy. This game has no proper subgame (each of the buyer's information sets contains a good-car node and a bad-car node), so SPE cannot narrow things down.

Reason about the buyer's beliefs:

  • Seeing the low price s_l: a good-car seller would lose by asking s_l (s_l-s_h<0) and would not do it. The sensible belief is "certainly a bad car". The buyer gets b_l-s_l>0 and buys.
  • Seeing the high price s_h: both kinds of seller like the high price (the bad-car seller even more), so the price carries no information and the belief stays half-half. Buying gives the buyer \frac{b_h+b_l}2-s_h in expectation.

Conclusion: if \frac{b_h+b_l}2\ge s_h, both kinds of car sell at s_h; if \frac{b_h+b_l}2<s_h, the buyer rejects the high price and only bad cars are sold: good cars are driven out of the market.

Numbers. b_h=10, s_h=8, b_l=4, s_l=2: \frac{10+4}2=7<8, good cars leave and only lemons remain. If b_h=14: \frac{14+4}2=9\ge8, and both kinds sell at 8.

12.2 Beliefs and behaviour strategies

  • Player i's belief \mu_i at an information set I: a probability for each node in I, \mu_i(N)=P(\text{at node }N\mid I\text{ reached}), summing to 1.
  • A behaviour strategy \sigma_i: probabilities over actions at each information set.
  • If \sigma gives every action positive probability (completely mixed), every information set is reached with positive probability and beliefs are uniquely given by Bayes' rule:
\mu(N_r)=\frac{P(N_r\mid\sigma)}{\sum_kP(N_k\mid\sigma)}.

Example. Player 1 goes left with 0.9 and right with 0.1, reaching player 2's information set \{A,B\}. Player 2's belief is \mu(A)=0.9, \mu(B)=0.1. If player 2 goes left with 0.9 at both nodes, the belief at the next information set \{C,D\} (C = left then left, D = right then left) is

\mu(C)=\frac{0.9\times0.9}{0.9\times0.9+0.1\times0.9}=\frac{0.81}{0.90}=0.9.

The difficulty. If an information set is not reached in equilibrium (probability 0), the denominator in Bayes' rule is 0 and the belief cannot be computed. It must then be specified separately.

12.3 Sequential rationality and perfect Bayesian equilibrium

Sequential rationality: at every information set, given his belief there and the others' strategies, the mover chooses a strategy that maximises his expected payoff.

Definition (perfect Bayesian equilibrium, PBE). A strategy profile \sigma and a belief system \mu form a PBE if:

  1. Sequential rationality: everyone is optimal at every information set (including unreached ones) given the beliefs there;
  2. Consistent beliefs: on the equilibrium path (information sets reached with positive probability) beliefs follow from \sigma by Bayes' rule; off the path, beliefs are derived from Bayes' rule and the equilibrium strategies wherever possible, and may be any distribution where that is impossible.

Relation to SPE. PBE extends "rational at every step" from subgames to information sets. In games of complete information it coincides with SPE. (Advanced: sequential equilibrium is a stricter version that requires beliefs to be limits of beliefs generated by completely mixed strategies, which also disciplines off-path beliefs.)

Example (off-path beliefs must be reasonable too). Player 1 chooses r (ending the game with (2, 0, 0)) or d. After d player 2 chooses L or R, and player 3, without seeing player 2's choice, chooses L′ or R′ at the information set \{D,E\}. Payoffs:

2 \ 3 L′ R′
L (1, 2, 1) (3, 3, 3)
R (0, 1, 2) (0, 1, 1)

Between players 2 and 3: L is strictly dominant for player 2 (2>1, 3>1); given L, player 3 chooses R′ (3>1). Subgame equilibrium (L, R′) with (3, 3, 3). Player 1 compares 3 from d and 2 from r and chooses d. The unique SPE is (d, L, R′); with the belief \mu(D)=1 it is also a PBE.

Another Nash equilibrium is (r, L, L′): player 1 chooses r and gets 2; switching to d would give only 1 under (L, L′), so she does not deviate. Player 3's information set is never reached, so it seems any belief will do, for instance \mu(D)=0 (believing player 2 chose R), under which L′ is optimal for player 3 (2>1). But PBE requires off-path beliefs to agree with the equilibrium strategies wherever possible: player 2's strategy is L (and L is dominant for him), so \mu(D)=1 is required, and then L′ is not optimal. (r, L, L′) is not a PBE.

12.4 Signalling games

Structure. Two players, a sender and a receiver.

  1. Nature draws the sender's type t\in T according to a prior p(t); the prior is common knowledge and only the sender sees the type.
  2. The sender, knowing his type, sends a message m\in M.
  3. The receiver sees the message (not the type) and chooses an action a\in A.
  4. Payoffs u_S(t,m,a) and u_R(t,m,a).
Model Sender (type) Message Receiver's action
market for lemons seller (car quality) asking price buy or not
Spence (1973) job market worker (productivity) education wage
Myers–Majluf (1984) firm (profitability of existing assets) equity stake offered invest or not

A pure-strategy PBE has three parts:

  • beliefs \mu(t\mid m): the probability of type t after seeing message m;
  • the receiver's action a^*(m): maximises \sum_t\mu(t\mid m)u_R(t,m,a) given the beliefs;
  • the sender's message m^*(t): anticipating a^*(\cdot), maximises u_S(t,m,a^*(m));

where beliefs satisfy Bayes' rule \mu(t\mid m)=\frac{p(t)}{\sum_{t'\text{ sending }m}p(t')} for messages sent by some type (on the path), and may be any distribution for messages nobody sends (off the path).

Equilibria come in two kinds: pooling (all types send the same message, which reveals nothing) and separating (different types send different messages, which reveal the type completely).

12.5 A complete example

Two types t_1,t_2, half each; messages L or R; actions u or d. Payoffs (sender, receiver):

Type (L, u) (L, d) (R, u) (R, d)
t_1 1, 3 4, 0 2, 1 0, 0
t_2 2, 4 0, 1 1, 0 1, 2

Let \mu = the belief in t_1 after L and \mu' = the belief in t_1 after R. Check the four possibilities one by one:

(1) Both send L (pooling on L). After L, \mu=0.5: u gives \frac{3+4}2=3.5, d gives \frac{0+1}2=0.5, so a(L)=u; t_1 gets 1 and t_2 gets 2. To stop t_1 switching to R we need a(R)=d (if a(R)=u, t_1 would get 2>1 from R). With a(R)=d, t_1 would get 0 and t_2 1 from R, so neither deviates. R is off the path, so \mu' can be chosen; the receiver picks d if and only if 2(1-\mu')\ge\mu', i.e. \mu'\le\frac23.

So [(L, L), (u, d), \mu=0.5, \mu'\le\frac23] is a pooling PBE.

(2) Both send R. After R, \mu'=0.5: u gives 0.5, d gives 1, so a(R)=d and t_1 gets 0. But t_1 gets at least 1 (u) or 4 (d) from L, so she surely deviates. Not an equilibrium.

(3) t_1 sends L, t_2 sends R. Beliefs \mu=1, \mu'=0. a(L)=u (3>0), a(R)=d (2>0). t_2 gets 1, but by sending L he would be taken for t_1, get u and earn 2. Not an equilibrium.

(4) t_1 sends R, t_2 sends L. Beliefs \mu=0, \mu'=1. a(L)=u (4>1), a(R)=u (1>0). t_1 gets 2 (only 1 from L) and t_2 gets 2 (only 1 from R); neither deviates.

So [(R, L), (u, u), \mu=0, \mu'=1] is a separating PBE.

12.6 Spence's job-market signalling model

Setting.

  • A worker has low productivity (l, probability p) or high productivity (h, probability 1-p), known only to himself.
  • The worker chooses years of education e\ge0. Education does not raise productivity, but it is harder for the low type: costs c(l,e)=e and c(h,e)=\frac e2.
  • Two firms see e (not productivity) and compete with wage offers; the worker goes to the higher one.
  • A low-productivity worker produces 1, a high-productivity worker 2.
  • The firms' belief: \mu(e) = probability that a worker with education e is the low type.

Wage = expected productivity. The two firms compete in wages like Bertrand competitors: if one offers less than expected output, the other offers a bit more and takes the worker. So in equilibrium

w(e)=\mu(e)\cdot1+(1-\mu(e))\cdot2=2-\mu(e).

Pooling equilibria. Both types choose the same education e^*, so \mu(e^*)=p and w(e^*)=2-p. Off the path set \mu(e)=1 for e<e^*, i.e. w(e)=1. The worker must prefer e^* to 0:

  • high type: 2-p-\frac{e^*}2\ge1\iff e^*\le2(1-p);
  • low type: 2-p-e^*\ge1\iff e^*\le1-p.

So any e^*\in[0,1-p] can be a pooling PBE.

Separating equilibria. The low type chooses e_l and the high type e_h\ne e_l. Beliefs \mu(e_l)=1, \mu(e_h)=0, wages w(e_l)=1, w(e_h)=2. Constraints:

  • low type participates: 1-e_l\ge1, so e_l=0;
  • high type participates: 2-\frac{e_h}2\ge1, so e_h\le2;
  • high type does not mimic the low type: 2-\frac{e_h}2\ge1, as above;
  • low type does not mimic the high type: 1\ge2-e_h, so e_h\ge1.

So e_l=0 and e_h\in[1,2]. With the belief "education below e_h means low type", this is a separating PBE.

Example. e_h=1: a low-type worker who studies for 1 year gets 2-1=1, the same as the 1 he gets without studying, so he does not study (it just fails to pay). A high-type worker who studies for 1 year gets 2-0.5=1.5>1, so he studies. Education separates the two types even though it adds nothing to productivity.

What makes a signal work. A credible signal must cost different types different amounts: the high type finds studying easier and is willing to prove himself with education, while for the low type imitation is too expensive. If studying were equally hard for both, education could not convey any information.

13. Recap: one storyline

The whole text follows two questions: who moves first, and who knows what?

Kind of game Equilibrium concept What it adds Examples
static, complete information Nash equilibrium everyone best-responds to the others prisoners' dilemma, Cournot, Bertrand
static, mixing mixed-strategy equilibrium probabilities make the opponent indifferent matching pennies, inspection
dynamic, complete information subgame perfect equilibrium equilibrium in every subgame (credible threats) Stackelberg, centipede, repeated games
static, incomplete information Bayesian Nash equilibrium every type best-responds in expectation sealed-bid auctions, double auction
dynamic, incomplete information perfect Bayesian equilibrium beliefs consistent with strategies, sequential rationality at every information set lemons, Spence signalling

Some economic lessons that run through the text:

  1. Individual rationality ≠ collective rationality: the prisoners' dilemma, public goods, the Cournot cartel, the centipede game.
  2. The details of the rules decide the outcome: prices or quantities, simultaneous or sequential, first or second price.
  3. Commitment has value, but it must be credible: first-mover advantage, announcing an inspection rate in advance, non-credible threats removed by SPE.
  4. Long relationships can sustain cooperation: repeated games and the folk theorem.
  5. Information is costly: good cars leave the lemons market, efficient trades fail in the double auction, signals cost real money.

14. Common misconceptions

Misconception Correct view
A Nash equilibrium is the best outcome A Nash equilibrium only means nobody wants to change alone; the equilibrium of the prisoners' dilemma is bad for everyone
Every game has a unique Nash equilibrium There may be several (the Battle of the Sexes has three), or no pure one (matching pennies)
A mixed strategy means "choose at random, anyhow" The mixing probabilities are computed exactly so as to make the opponent indifferent between his options
In a mixed equilibrium my probabilities depend on my payoffs The opposite: my probabilities are pinned down by the opponent's payoffs (in the inspection game the fine does not affect the pollution probability)
The order of eliminating dominated strategies does not matter With weakly dominated strategies the order can change the result; only elimination of strictly dominated strategies is order-independent
Moving first is always an advantage Leading pays in quantity competition and hurts in price competition; in preemption games the first-mover advantage is competed away
Two firms are not enough for competition In the Bertrand model two firms push the price down to cost; product differences, cost differences and capacity limits change this
A threat works as long as it is announced Only threats one would actually carry out when the moment comes are credible (subgame perfection)
Repetition always sustains cooperation With a unique stage equilibrium, finite repetition cannot sustain cooperation; infinite repetition or several stage equilibria are needed
First-price auctions raise more because the winner pays his own bid Bidders shade their bids; under the conditions of revenue equivalence all auctions raise the same expected revenue
Beliefs at unreached information sets can be anything PBE requires off-path beliefs to agree with the equilibrium strategies wherever possible, and off-path beliefs shape on-path behaviour
Education must pay because it raises productivity In signalling models education conveys information even if it is useless in production, as long as it costs different types different amounts

15. Exercises with answers

Exercise 1 (dominant strategies). Two firms choose to advertise (A) or not (N). Payoffs: (A, A) = (3, 3), (A, N) = (6, 1), (N, A) = (1, 6), (N, N) = (5, 5). Find the dominant-strategy equilibrium. Is it efficient?

Answer. If the rival chooses A, A gives 3 > 1 from N; if the rival chooses N, A gives 6 > 5. A is dominant and the equilibrium (A, A) gives (3, 3), Pareto dominated by (N, N) with (5, 5); it is inefficient. A prisoners' dilemma.

Exercise 2 (Nash equilibrium). Find all pure-strategy Nash equilibria of the game below.

1 \ 2 L C R
T 2, 1 0, 0 1, 2
M 1, 1 1, 3 0, 0
B 0, 0 3, 1 2, 2

Answer. Player 1's best responses: T against L (2), B against C (3), B against R (2). Player 2's best responses: R against T (2), C against M (3), R against B (2). The doubly best cell is (B, R) with (2, 2). It is the only one.

Exercise 3 (mixed strategies). Find the mixed equilibrium of the game below.

1 \ 2 L R
U 3, 1 0, 2
D 1, 3 2, 0

Answer. There is no pure equilibrium. Let player 1 play U with p and player 2 play L with q. Player 2 indifferent: 1\cdot p+3(1-p)=2p, so 3-2p=2p and p=\frac34. Player 1 indifferent: 3q=q+2(1-q), so 3q=2-q and q=\frac12. Equilibrium (p,q)=(\frac34,\frac12). Player 1 expects 3\times\frac12=1.5 and player 2 expects 2\times\frac34=1.5.

Exercise 4 (inspection). In the inspection game of Section 4.5 let F=5 and C=1. Find the mixed equilibrium. If the fine rises to F=10, how do the probabilities of pollution and inspection change?

Answer. p^*=C/5=0.2 and q^*=1/F=0.2. With F=10, q^*=0.1 and p^* is still 0.2. Doubling the fine halves the inspection rate and leaves the pollution probability unchanged.

Exercise 5 (Cournot). Demand P=100-Q, both firms have marginal cost 10. Find the Cournot outputs, price and profits, and the profits under collusion (splitting the monopoly output).

Answer. a-c=90. Cournot: each produces 90/3=30, Q=60, P=40, profit 30\times30=900. Monopoly: Q=45, P=55, total profit 45\times45=2025; split, 1012.5 each > 900.

Exercise 6 (Stackelberg). Same as above, with firm 1 moving first. Find both outputs and profits.

Answer. q_1=\frac{90}2=45, q_2=\frac{90-45}2=22.5, P=100-67.5=32.5. \pi_1=22.5\times45=1012.5 and \pi_2=22.5\times22.5=506.25.

Exercise 7 (Hotelling). In the linear city c=4 and t=3. Find the equilibrium prices and profits. If firm 1 charges 7 and firm 2 charges 8, where is the indifferent consumer?

Answer. p^*=c+t=7 and each earns (7-4)\times\frac12=1.5. x^*=\frac{8-7}{6}+\frac12=\frac23: firm 1 gets two-thirds of the market.

Exercise 8 (backward induction). An incumbent faces a potential entrant. The entrant chooses "enter" or "stay out" (staying out: entrant 0, incumbent 10). After entry the incumbent chooses "price war" (entrant −2, incumbent 2) or "accommodate" (entrant 3, incumbent 4). Find the SPE. Is "I will certainly start a price war" a credible threat?

Answer. After entry the incumbent compares 2 and 4 and accommodates. The entrant expects 3 > 0 and enters. SPE: (enter; accommodate) with (3, 4). The price-war threat is not credible: when it comes to it, a price war gives the incumbent 2 < 4. ("Stay out / price war if entry" is a Nash equilibrium but not subgame perfect.)

Exercise 9 (grim trigger). Prisoners' dilemma: both cooperate 3 each, both defect 1 each, a lone defector gets 5 and the betrayed player 0. For which \delta is grim trigger an SPE?

Answer. Conforming gives \frac3{1-\delta}; deviating gives 5+\frac{\delta}{1-\delta}. We need 3\ge5(1-\delta)+\delta=5-4\delta, i.e. \delta\ge\frac12.

Exercise 10 (two stage equilibria). In the pricing game of Section 10.3, if the discount factor between the two periods is \delta=0.4, is "(H, H) in period 1, then reward (M, M) or punishment (L, L) in period 2" still an SPE?

Answer. No. Conforming gives 8+6\times0.4=10.4; deviating gives 10+2\times0.4=10.8>10.4. It requires \delta\ge0.5.

Exercise 11 (first-price auction). Three bidders with values independent and uniform on [0,1]. What is the equilibrium bid? What is the seller's expected revenue? Compare with the second-price auction.

Answer. b(v)=\frac23v. The highest value z has P(z\le x)=x^3, so E[z]=\int_0^13x^3dx=\frac34 and first-price revenue is \frac23\times\frac34=\frac12. Second-price revenue is the expected second-highest value: the k-th smallest of n uniform variables has expectation \frac k{n+1}, and the second-highest is the 2nd smallest when n=3, with expectation \frac24=\frac12. Equal, as revenue equivalence predicts.

Exercise 12 (second-price auction). In a second-price auction your value is 50 and the highest other bid is 40. What do you get by bidding 45, 50 or 60? What if the highest other bid is 55?

Answer. Highest other bid 40: bidding 45, 50 or 60 all win and pay 40, earning 10. Highest other bid 55: bidding 45 or 50 loses, earning 0; bidding 60 wins, pays 55 and earns −5. Bidding your value is never worse than any other bid.

Exercise 13 (Bayesian updating). In a lemons market 30% of cars are good and 70% bad. Good-car sellers always ask a high price and bad-car sellers ask it with probability \frac12. After seeing a high price, what probability should the buyer attach to a good car?

Answer. P(\text{high})=0.3\times1+0.7\times0.5=0.65. P(\text{good}\mid\text{high})=\frac{0.3}{0.65}=\frac6{13}\approx0.46.

Exercise 14 (Spence). In the model of Section 12.6 let p=0.5. Which education levels can form a pooling equilibrium? Which a separating one? In a separating equilibrium, which e_h is best for the high type?

Answer. Pooling: e^*\in[0,1-p]=[0,0.5]. Separating: e_l=0, e_h\in[1,2]. The high type's payoff 2-\frac{e_h}2 falls with e_h, so e_h=1 is best (payoff 1.5): it is the "cheapest" separating equilibrium.

Term Meaning

rent equalisation competition reduces the first-mover advantage to zero in equilibrium
